blocks.title: Cis-trans isomers
blocks.text: Cis-trans isomers are stereoisomers with different spatial arrangements of atoms because rotation about a double bond in an open-chain compound is restricted.

First consider butane. Rotation about the C2-C3 single bond turns one arrangement of the methyl groups into another. Such forms are conformational isomers: they interconvert freely by rotation about the C-C single bond and cannot be separated at room temperature.

blocks.alt: Two drawings of butane, I and II, joined by an arrow with a rotation sign. In I, carbon 2 carries CH3 (carbon 1) at the upper left and two H; carbon 3 carries two H and CH3 (carbon 4) at the lower right. In II, rotation about the C2-C3 bond has moved carbon 1 to the lower left (H3C), with H at the upper left and left; carbon 3 is unchanged.
blocks.caption: Two forms (I and II) of butane interconverted by rotation about the C2-C3 single bond (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.text: In but-2-ene, CH3-CH=CH-CH3, carbons 2 and 3 are sp2 hybridised. The C=C double bond consists of a sigma bond, formed by end-on overlap of sp2 hybrid orbitals, and a pi bond, formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals. The pi bond locks the molecule: the two carbons of the double bond and the groups attached to them lie in one plane and are fixed in space. To rotate about the double bond the pi bond would have to break, which needs about 263 kJ/mol, not available at room temperature. This restricted rotation is the origin of cis-trans isomerism.

blocks.alt: Three drawings of but-2-ene, p orbitals as blue lobes. Cis: two C joined, each with lobes up and down overlapping above and below (the pi bond, with an electron pair); H on hashed bonds at the top, H3C and CH3 on wedges below. Middle: one carbon turned through 90 degrees so its p orbital is perpendicular to the other, each lobe with one electron: no overlap with the ends perpendicular. Trans: like cis but CH3 top right and H bottom right. Crossed double arrows between them.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.6: The two isomers of but-2-ene cannot interconvert by rotation about the C-C double bond without breaking the pi bond (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.6).

blocks.alt: Two structural formulae: cis-but-2-ene, C=C with H3C and CH3 both at the top and H and H at the bottom; trans-but-2-ene, C=C with H and CH3 at the top and H3C and H at the bottom.
blocks.caption: Cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

items: Cis isomer: the two similar groups are on the same side of the double bond (cis-but-2-ene).
Trans isomer: the two similar groups are on opposite sides (trans-but-2-ene).
Cis-trans isomerism is not possible if either carbon of the double bond carries two identical groups, e.g. but-1-ene (CH2=CH-CH2CH3) and 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene ((CH3)2C=C(CH3)2).

blocks.title: Condition for cis-trans isomerism
blocks.text: An open-chain compound shows cis-trans isomerism if it has a double bond and each carbon of the double bond carries two different groups.

blocks.title: Keep in mind
blocks.text: Cis and trans isomers have different physical and chemical properties: different melting and boiling points, dipole moments, densities and heats of vaporisation. The trans isomer is usually more stable than the cis isomer, so their reactivity differs too.
